thread.title_full: Home appraisals going up 19% in one county. How will that impact taxes? - NewsBreak

author: Victoria Moorwood
title: Home appraisals going up 19% in one county. How will that impact taxes? - NewsBreak
text:
By Victoria Moorwood ,
1 days ago
Some homeowners in a suburban Cincinnati county will see their property values increase by almost 20% this year.
Butler County property owners will receive a letter with their home's updated appraisal later this year. County auditors conduct a full reappraisal of properties every six years and update each appraisal every three years based on market data.
The median value increase across Butler County is 19% for 2026, Auditor Nancy Nix said in a press release this week. Municipalities' median increase ranged between 12 and 39%.
"Due to global and national factors, inflation in the residential real estate market over the past six years has been extremely high," Nix said in the release. "But the new laws passed by the Legislature will prevent the huge tax increases many saw following the 2023 triennial update."
Ohio home values have skyrocketed in recent years. In 2023, the year of Butler County's last full reappraisal, property values soared by 37% , the largest increase among Greater Cincinnati counties.
How much could my property value go up? The increase in property value depends on the township or city you live in. Here are the median value increases in Butler County jurisdictions, according to Nix:
Lemon Township: 39%. New Miami: 32%. Millville: 31%. Middletown: 30%. Wayne Township: 29%. Reily Township: 28%. Hamilton: 27%. Milford Township: 26%. Sharonville: 24%. St. Clair Township: 23%. Trenton: 22%. Ross Township: 20%. Morgan Township: 19%. Liberty Township: 18%. West Chester Township: 18%. Hanover Township: 17%. Fairfield Township: 15%. Madison Township: 15%. Monroe: 15%. Oxford: 15% Oxford Township: 15%. Fairfield: 12%. Median value refers to the halfway point among one area's values. It does not mean your home's value will increase by that exact percentage.
Each residential and agricultural property owner will receive a letter with their home's new appraised value later this year.
How do increased property values impact taxes? Property taxes mostly go toward schools but also help pay for police, libraries and infrastructure projects. Higher property values don't necessarily mean higher taxes ‒ schools and levies play a role .
Some Greater Cincinnati school districts have reached what state legislators call the 20-mill floor, which guarantees a certain amount of revenue for schools. One mill represents $1 for every $1,000 of a home's assessed value.
Property tax rates can't go down if that would cause a school's direct millage to fall below 20 mills. So, if your home's appraised value goes up and you live in a school district that has hit the 20-mill floor, you may see a rise in property tax.
Voter-passed levies also add to property taxes. However, state law requires most of them to bring in only a specific amount of money. For example, voters could approve a levy that brings in $10 million per year. As property values go up, the tax rate for that levy is lowered so the levy would still bring in $10 million.
In May, voters approved new levies that will show up in property tax bills next year, including:
A countywide Board of Developmental Disabilities levy that will increase taxes by about $70 per $100,000 of a home's value. A fire district levy in Fairfield Township that will increase taxes by about $157 per $100,000 in property value. A fire and EMS levy in Milford Township that will cost about $70 per $100,000 of a home's value. Voters could also pass other levies in November.
County previously passed 'piggyback' homestead tax break Butler County's three Republican commissioners voted in 2025 to offer its own homestead property tax exemption that "piggybacks" on the state's homestead program . The "piggyback" provision, which allows eligible homeowners to get both tax breaks, was passed in the 2026-2027 Ohio budget .
The homestead exemption is available for people with disabilities and seniors whose total income falls below a certain amount. The exemption reduces the amount of a home's value that is taxed by $28,000. That means an eligible homeowner whose house is valued at $100,000 will pay property taxes as if their home were valued at $72,000.
The doubled exemption means eligible homeowners in Butler County can reduce their home's value by $56,000.
Butler County was the first Ohio county to adopt the doubled exemption, saving taxpayers ‒ and costing schools and the county ‒ millions of dollars.
This article originally appeared on Cincinnati Enquirer: Home appraisals going up 19% in one county. How will that impact taxes?
